hindi: दुर्योधन कहता है: “भीष्म की रक्षा में हमारी सेना हमारे लिए बहुत बड़ी है (या: काफ़ी नहीं है), और भीम की रक्षा में उनकी सेना छोटी है (या: काफ़ी है)।” इन शब्दों के दो अर्थ हो सकते हैं, और दोनों में उसके मन की बेचैनी झलकती है।
english: Duryodhana says: “This army of ours, guarded by Bhishma, is unlimited (or, some read, not enough). That army of theirs, guarded by Bhima, is limited (or, some read, enough).” The word can be read two ways, and both readings show what is going on in his mind.
deeper: The Sanskrit word aparyāptam can mean “unlimited, immeasurable” or “not enough, insufficient.” Great teachers have understood the verse in both ways. Either Duryodhana is boasting that his army is too big to count, or his worry is slipping out and he is admitting that Bhishma’s protection may not be enough.

Notice what he is doing. He is counting soldiers and comparing sizes. He trusts numbers, big names and weapons. He does not ask whether his side is doing what is right. When we only measure strength and never ask about goodness, we often feel shaky inside, however loudly we talk.

The verse teaches us to listen to our own words. Sometimes we speak very boldly because we are a little afraid. Real confidence is quiet and comes from doing the right thing and preparing well. Boasting is often a way to cover up fear.
words: unlimited, immeasurable (or, in another reading, not enough)
limited, measurable (or, in another reading, enough)
background: On the field of Kurukshetra, two great armies stood facing each other, ready for the war. Duryodhana, the Kaurava prince, saw the Pandava army arranged in battle formation and went to his teacher Drona. He pointed out the Pandava warriors (1.2–1.6) and then named the great heroes on his own side (1.7–1.8).

He then added that many other brave soldiers were ready to give up their lives for him, all skilled with many weapons (1.9). Now, in verse 10, he sums it all up. He compares the two armies, his own guarded by the elder Bhishma and the Pandava army guarded by the mighty Bhima.
lessons: Loud boasting can sometimes be a sign that we are feeling unsure inside.
A big team or a famous name does not guarantee that we are on the right path.
Don’t compare only to feel safe
Counting other people’s strengths all the time can make us more anxious, not less.
Honest effort and a clear heart give us a calm courage that shouting cannot give.
One sentence can carry both pride and fear, so we should look carefully at what we really mean.
examples: Rohan shouts, “Our team will crush them!” before the match, but he keeps glancing at the other team’s tall bowler. His loud words are covering a little nervousness.
Priya tells everyone, “I don’t even need to study.” Inside, she is worried about the maths test. She feels better after she admits it and opens her book.
Kabir counts how many prizes his rival has won instead of finishing his own picture. When he stops comparing and starts colouring, he feels calmer.
Ananya says, “Singing in front of everyone is nothing!” but her hands are cold. Her friend says, “It’s okay to be nervous,” and she relaxes.
Imran’s team has more players than the other side, so the boys think they have already won. They forget to practise passing and lose the match.
Devika says, “My brother is the school captain, so nobody can beat me.” But the race is about her own running, not her brother’s fame.
Sameer keeps saying, “I’m sure to win!” whenever he is actually behind. His grandmother smiles and says, “Play well and let the game speak.”
Lakshmi says, “I’m a bit scared of the quiz, but I’ve prepared.” Her honesty makes her feel lighter, and she does better than the loud boasters.

story.title: Meera and the Kabaddi Match
paras: Meera was the captain of her school kabaddi team in a small town in Maharashtra. Before the big match against the neighbouring school, she stood in front of her team and said loudly, “We are the best! They have no chance at all!”

But as the other team walked in, Meera went quiet. She began counting their tall players and their strong raiders. Her voice had been big, but her heart was thumping. She told herself that numbers decided everything.

Her coach, Sunita Didi, noticed and took her aside. “Meera, you spoke very loudly just now. Are you worried?” Meera nodded. Didi said, “Then let’s say it plainly. We cannot control how tall they are. We can only control how well we play together.”

Meera told her team the truth: “I’m a little nervous, and I think we all are. Let’s stay together and do what we practised.” The team smiled and relaxed. They played carefully, and whether they won or lost, they played with calm hearts and proud faces.
story.moral: Lesson: Loud boasting often hides worry. Honest effort and a calm heart give a much steadier kind of strength.

quiz.q: Who does Duryodhana say is protecting his army in this verse?
quiz.x: He says his army is guarded by Bhishma, while the Pandava army is guarded by Bhima.

quiz.q: What can the word aparyāptam mean?
quiz.x: Aparyāptam can mean “unlimited” or “not enough,” so the verse can be read in two ways.

quiz.q: What does Duryodhana’s way of speaking show us?
o: He trusts numbers and strength, and may be hiding some worry
quiz.x: He compares army strength and talks boldly, but his words also hint at inner unease.

quiz.q: What is a good thing to do when we feel nervous before a contest?
o: Admit it honestly and focus on our preparation
Count only the other team’s strengths
quiz.x: Honesty about our feelings and good preparation give us calm, real confidence.

reel.hook: Ever talked big because you were secretly scared?
reel.lesson: Loud boasting often hides worry; calm preparation gives real confidence.
reel.caption:
Duryodhana counted armies and talked big, but his words hinted at worry. 🛡️
When we feel nervous, honesty and practice beat boasting every time.
What helps you feel calm before a big day? 💛
